Stammering
stam'er-ing
adj. (halting or unintelligible in speech; in Isaiah the foreign tongue that becomes a sign of judgment on those who would not hear plain words)
From stammer, Old English stamerian, to stutter. The Hebrew laeg in Isaiah 28:11 means mocking or barbarous speech — language that sounds like nonsense to the hearer, not a speech impediment in the speaker.

Biblical Definition

Isaiah is answering drunken priests and prophets who had mocked his preaching as baby-talk — precept upon precept, line upon line, here a little and there a little. His reply is a sentence of judgment: “For with stammering lips and another tongue will he speak to this people” (Isaiah 28:11). Since they would not hear the prophet's plain Hebrew, God would address them in Assyrian — the speech of an invading army, unintelligible and terrifying. The tragedy is stated in the next verse: “To whom he said, This is the rest wherewith ye may cause the weary to rest; and this is the refreshing: yet they would not hear” (Isaiah 28:12). Rest was offered in words they understood and refused; judgment came in words they could not understand. Isaiah repeats the figure later: “Thou shalt not see a fierce people, a people of a deeper speech than thou canst perceive; of a stammering tongue, that thou canst not understand” (Isaiah 33:19). Paul cites the passage in the tongues controversy at Corinth: “In the law it is written, With men of other tongues and other lips will I speak unto this people; and yet for all that will they not hear me, saith the Lord” (1 Corinthians 14:21).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines stammering as speaking with stops or hesitation, and to stammer as to stop in speaking or to speak with involuntary breaks.

expand to see more

STAMMERING, ppr. Speaking with stops or difficulty; hesitating.

STAMMER, v.i. To stop in uttering syllables or words; to hesitate or falter in speaking.

BARBAROUS, a. Foreign; in the Greek sense, a foreigner, one who speaks a language not understood.

UNINTELLIGIBLE, a. That cannot be understood.

REFRESHING, n. Refreshment; relief after fatigue or suffering.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 28:11 — "For with stammering lips and another tongue will he speak to this people."

Isaiah 28:12 — "To whom he said, This is the rest wherewith ye may cause the weary to rest; and this is the refreshing: yet they would not hear."

1 Corinthians 14:21 — "In the law it is written, With men of other tongues and other lips will I speak unto this people; and yet for all that will they not hear me, saith the Lord."

Isaiah 33:19 — "Thou shalt not see a fierce people, a people of a deeper speech than thou canst perceive; of a stammering tongue, that thou canst not understand."

Modern Corruption

Isaiah 28:11 is quoted as a promise of tongues-speaking, when Paul cites it in the same chapter where he uses it to restrain the practice.

expand to see more

1 Corinthians 14:21 is regularly produced as scriptural warrant for tongues in the assembly. Paul's use of it runs the other way. He quotes Isaiah's sentence of judgment and draws the conclusion in the very next verse: tongues are for a sign, not to them that believe, but to them that believe not. His whole argument in the chapter is for intelligibility — five words with understanding are worth more than ten thousand in an unknown tongue — and he grounds it in a passage where unintelligible speech was a curse on a people who would not hear. Whatever a reader concludes about the continuance of the gift, quoting this verse in favour of unrestrained tongues reverses the argument of the apostle who quoted it first.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Isaiah 28:12, one of the saddest verses in the prophets. God had spoken plainly, and what He said was this is the rest… this is the refreshing — and they would not hear. The judgment of unintelligible speech was measured to the refusal: they had called the prophet's clear words infantile babbling, and God gave them real babbling from an army. There is a warning here for congregations that find plain preaching dull. Clarity offered and despised is not a neutral event, and God has more than one way of speaking to a people who will not hear the first.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew laeg, mocking or barbarous speech — Isaiah 28:11; illeg, stammering — Isaiah 32:4; amoq saphah, deep of lip — Isaiah 33:19; Greek heteroglossos (G2084) — 1 Corinthians 14:21.

expand to see more

Hebrew laeg — mocking, stammering, barbarous; Isaiah 28:11, of the foreign tongue God would use.

Hebrew illeg — stammering; Isaiah 32:4, where the stammerer shall speak plainly in the restoration.

Hebrew amoq saphah — deep of lip, of speech too deep to perceive; Isaiah 33:19.

Greek heteroglossos (G2084) — of another tongue; 1 Corinthians 14:21, its only occurrence.

1 Corinthians 14:22 draws Paul's own conclusion: tongues are for a sign, not to them that believe, but to them that believe not.

Usage

"“With stammering lips and another tongue will he speak to this people” — a sentence, not a promise."

"“This is the rest… yet they would not hear” — clarity offered and despised."

"They called plain preaching baby-talk, and God sent them an army they could not understand."
